paragraphs: Swamiji had a friend in America, a well-known scientist, who loved reading about the Buddha's life. But one thing bothered him: the Buddha died peacefully in old age. He hadn't been crucified! Swamiji found this a very strange idea, as if a person can only be truly great if he is killed for it. That way of thinking, he said, never took hold in India.
The Buddha walked across India speaking against her gods, even against the idea of a God of the universe. Yet he lived to eighty and won over half the country.

India also had the Charvakas, who taught the most blunt, open materialism, harsher than anything people in the nineteenth century dared to preach openly. They went from temple to temple and city to city saying religion was nonsense and a trick by priests, that the Vedas were written by fools, rogues and demons, and that there was no God and no eternal soul. If a soul existed, they asked, why did it never return after death, drawn back by love for wife and child? If it did survive, wouldn't it still want good food and fine clothes? Even so, nobody harmed them.

This, said Swamiji, shows India's great tradition of religious freedom. And freedom is the first condition for growth. Whatever is not set free will never grow. The belief that you can make others grow by directing and controlling them, while keeping all the freedom for yourself as the teacher, is a dangerous lie. It has held back millions upon millions of people. Give people the light of liberty, he said; that alone lets them grow.
learn: People and ideas grow best when they are free to question, even to disagree loudly. Real teachers and leaders guide without controlling. Defend the freedom of others to think differently, and protect your own.
